articles.label: Hurricane Season
articles.headline: Escambia County's new evacuation zones go into effect June 1. Here's what changed.
articles.dek: FEMA flood map updates have redrawn who evacuates when. Some neighborhoods that rode out Ivan are now in Zone A.
brief: New evacuation zone maps take effect June 1, reclassifying thousands of Escambia County properties based on updated FEMA flood data.
Parts of Myrtle Grove, Warrington, and areas near Bayou Texar have shifted from Zone B to Zone A, requiring evacuation for Category 1 storms.
Residents can check their new zone designation at the county's Know Your Zone portal or by calling 311.
articles.body:
The laminated evacuation map that hung on Deborah Sutton's refrigerator for twenty years showed her Myrtle Grove home in Zone B. She never left for anything less than a Category 3.

That map is now wrong.

Starting June 1, Escambia County's revised evacuation zones take effect. The changes follow FEMA's updated Flood Insurance Rate Maps, finalized last October after a multi-year study. The new boundaries reflect post-Hurricane Sally drainage patterns, sea level measurements, and storm surge modeling that didn't exist when the previous zones were drawn in 2004.

Sutton's house on Lillian Highway is now Zone A. So are roughly 4,200 other Escambia County properties that previously sat in Zone B, according to county emergency management figures.

"We rode out Ivan in this house," Sutton said. "Now they're telling me I have to leave for a Cat 1? That's a hard adjustment."

What the zones mean

Escambia County uses five evacuation zones, labeled A through E. Zone A evacuates first, typically for Category 1 hurricanes or strong tropical storms with significant surge potential. Zone E evacuates only for the most catastrophic scenarios.

The zones don't measure wind risk. They measure drowning risk.

"People confuse this with hurricane categories, and that's dangerous," said Eric Gilmore, Escambia County's emergency management director. "A Category 1 storm hitting at high tide on a certain trajectory can push eight feet of water into Zone A neighborhoods. That kills people."

The previous zone maps were based on 2004 FEMA data, drawn months after Hurricane Ivan. They relied on elevation surveys and storm surge models that predated LIDAR mapping technology now standard in flood analysis.

Who moved where

The most significant shifts occurred in three areas:

Myrtle Grove: Approximately 1,800 properties along the Perdido Bay shoreline and interior canals moved from Zone B to Zone A. The area saw substantial flooding during Hurricane Sally in 2020, which emergency officials say validated the reclassification.

Warrington: Neighborhoods south of Navy Boulevard and west of Pace Boulevard, roughly 1,400 properties, shifted from B to A. The changes reflect updated modeling of Bayou Grande surge behavior.

East Pensacola Heights and Bayou Texar: About 1,000 properties near the bayou's northern fingers moved into Zone A. Several streets that flooded during Sally had been classified Zone B for two decades.

Smaller pockets of Zone C properties across the county also shifted to Zone B, though these changes affect evacuation timing less dramatically.

Some residents saw their zones decrease. Approximately 600 properties in higher-elevation areas of Brent and Brownsville moved from Zone B to Zone C after updated elevation data showed less surge vulnerability than previously modeled.

The Ivan problem

Emergency management officials acknowledge they're fighting twenty years of muscle memory.

Hurricane Ivan made landfall in September 2004 as a Category 3 storm. It devastated Pensacola Beach and caused widespread wind damage across the county. But its storm surge, while severe on the barrier islands, didn't reach many Zone A and B neighborhoods on the mainland the way models predicted.

"Ivan taught a lot of people the wrong lessons," Gilmore said. "They stayed, and their house didn't flood, so they thought their house doesn't flood. That's not how surge works."

Hurricane Sally in 2020 provided a corrective. The Category 2 storm stalled over the area, dumping historic rainfall. But it also pushed surge into mainland neighborhoods that Ivan had spared. Myrtle Grove, Warrington, and areas near Bayou Texar saw water in homes that had stayed dry for decades.

"Sally was the storm we modeled for," said Jennifer Walsh, a FEMA flood plain specialist who worked on the Escambia County map revision. "It validated a lot of what the new modeling showed."

What it means for residents

The zone change doesn't automatically affect flood insurance rates. FEMA flood zones and county evacuation zones serve different purposes, though they're based on similar data. Residents should check both their evacuation zone and their flood zone designation separately.

The evacuation zone change does mean new obligations during storm events. When the county issues a Zone A evacuation order, residents in newly designated Zone A areas will be expected to leave. Those who don't face no legal penalty, but they also won't receive emergency rescue services once conditions deteriorate.

"We're not going to arrest anyone for staying," Gilmore said. "But we're also not sending first responders into surge conditions to rescue people who chose to ride it out. That's been the policy, and it's not changing."

The county is distributing new Know Your Zone materials through libraries, community centers, and the annual hurricane guide mailed to all county addresses in late May. An interactive map at KnowYourZoneFL.com allows residents to enter their address and see their current designation.

Sutton, the Myrtle Grove resident, said she understands the reasoning. She just doesn't like it.

"I've got three dogs and a mother-in-law who doesn't travel well," she said. "Evacuating is a whole production. But I guess if they're telling me the water's coming, I better listen."

The new zones take effect June 1, the official start of Atlantic hurricane season.

articles.label: Pensacola Beach
articles.headline: The fight over paid parking at Pensacola Beach enters its third summer
articles.dek: Santa Rosa Island Authority says revenue covers beach services. Critics say it prices out locals. Both have receipts.
brief: Santa Rosa Island Authority collected $4.2 million in parking revenue last fiscal year, up from $3.1 million in the program's first year
Beach attendance data shows weekday visits down 18% since paid parking began, while weekend numbers remain flat
A citizen petition calling for a parking fee cap has gathered 3,400 signatures ahead of the June SRIA board meeting
articles.body:
The woman in the burgundy minivan circled the Casino Beach lot three times before she found a spot. Then she sat there, phone in hand, for another four minutes.

"Twenty dollars," said Maria Fontaine, a Navy spouse from Warrington. "Twenty dollars to park at a public beach." She paid it anyway. Her kids were already unbuckled in the back seat, and she'd promised them the afternoon.

This scene plays out hundreds of times daily along Pensacola Beach's public access points, now entering the third summer of the Santa Rosa Island Authority's paid parking program. What began as a pilot initiative in 2024 has become the most contentious local policy debate in Escambia County—a fight over who owns the beach experience and who should pay for it.

The money trail

SRIA's numbers tell one story. The authority collected $4.2 million in parking revenue last fiscal year, a 35% increase over the program's $3.1 million debut. That money funds lifeguard salaries, beach cleaning equipment, restroom maintenance, and the trolley service that runs from the Visitor's Center to Fort Pickens Road.

"Before paid parking, we were running a $1.8 million annual deficit on beach services," said SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio at the board's April meeting. "Escambia County taxpayers were subsidizing every out-of-state visitor who used our beaches. That equation has flipped."

The authority's financial reports show beach operations now generate a $600,000 annual surplus, money the board has earmarked for dune restoration and a new lifeguard headquarters.

Critics don't dispute the revenue figures. They dispute who's paying them.

The local cost

A coalition calling itself Free Our Beach has spent two years tracking what they say the SRIA won't: the demographic shift in who actually uses Pensacola Beach.

Their data, compiled from SRIA's own gate counts and surveys conducted at beach access points, suggests weekday attendance has dropped 18% since paid parking began. Weekend numbers remain essentially flat. The group's interpretation: locals who once visited casually on Tuesday afternoons have been priced out. Tourists, who planned and budgeted for the trip anyway, keep coming.

"The beach used to be where Pensacola went after work," said Derek Hollis, a Pensacola firefighter and Free Our Beach organizer. "Now it's a destination. That's a fundamental change to how this community relates to its own coastline."

The current rate structure charges $5 per hour with a $20 daily maximum at Casino Beach and Quietwater. Rates drop to $3 per hour at lots east of Portofino. Annual passes cost $150 for Escambia and Santa Rosa county residents, $300 for everyone else.

Free Our Beach's petition, which has gathered 3,400 signatures, calls for a $10 daily cap for Florida residents and free parking after 5 p.m. year-round. The group plans to present it at the SRIA's June 12 board meeting.

The legal question nobody wants to answer

Underneath the policy debate sits an unresolved legal question: Can the SRIA charge for beach parking at all?

The authority operates under a 1947 lease from Escambia County that grants it control of Santa Rosa Island's developed areas. That lease requires the SRIA to maintain "free and open public access" to the beach. Whether paid parking violates that clause has never been tested in court.

Escambia County Attorney Alison Rogers declined to offer an opinion on the lease language when asked at a County Commission meeting in March. "That would be a matter for litigation to determine," she said.

Free Our Beach has consulted with attorneys but hasn't filed suit. Hollis said the group prefers a political solution. "We'd rather win this at the ballot box than in a courtroom," he said.

The SRIA's position is that parking infrastructure—the lots, the meters, the enforcement—falls outside the lease's public access requirements. "The beach is free," Ghio said. "Parking is a service we provide."

What the tourists say

At the pavilion near the fishing pier on a recent Saturday, the complaints came from unexpected directions.

"I've been coming here from Birmingham for fifteen years," said Ronald Atchison, setting up a canopy with his wife. "Used to be, this was the affordable beach. Gulf Shores got expensive, Orange Beach got expensive, and Pensacola was still Pensacola." He shook his head. "Twenty dollars to park, fourteen dollars for a burger. It's not what it was."

But others shrugged off the fees. "We paid eighty dollars a day to park at Disney," said Jennifer Moody, visiting from suburban Atlanta with her family. "This is nothing."

The SRIA doesn't track visitor origin data in a way that would show whether parking fees have affected the tourism mix. VisitPensacola, the county's tourism marketing arm, reported record hotel occupancy rates for spring break 2026 but declined to attribute the numbers to any specific factor.

The summer ahead

Memorial Day weekend will mark the unofficial start of the third paid parking summer. The SRIA has added 200 spaces at a new lot near the Boardwalk and installed additional pay stations to reduce lines. Enforcement officers will patrol seven days a week through Labor Day.

The June board meeting is expected to draw a crowd. Free Our Beach has organized carpools from the mainland. A countergroup, Support Our Shores, has emerged on social media arguing that parking revenue protects the beach from overdevelopment. Their membership is smaller but vocal.

Maria Fontaine, the Navy spouse from the Casino Beach lot, said she hasn't decided whether to buy an annual pass this year. "A hundred fifty dollars is a lot when you don't know if you'll be stationed here next summer," she said.

Her kids were already running toward the water. She grabbed the cooler and followed them.

The beach was free. The parking wasn't.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Gate wait times at NAS Pensacola are averaging 45 minutes. The Navy says help is coming.
articles.dek: A staffing shortage at the main gate has base workers clocking in late and missing appointments. A new credentialing system is months away.
brief: Wait times at NAS Pensacola's main gate have averaged 45 minutes during morning rush since March, with some commuters reporting delays exceeding an hour.
The delays stem from a 30% staffing shortage among contracted security personnel, compounded by increased credential verification requirements implemented in January.
Navy officials say a new automated credentialing system will be operational by September, but workers and contractors say they need relief now.
articles.body:
At 6:47 a.m. on a Tuesday, the line of cars waiting to enter NAS Pensacola stretches back past the Waffle House on Navy Boulevard. Brake lights glow red in the predawn dark. A woman in scrubs drums her fingers on the steering wheel of a silver Camry. She's due at the Naval Hospital at 7. She will not make it.

"I've started telling patients to expect me 15 minutes late," said the woman, a civilian nurse who asked not to be named because she wasn't authorized to speak publicly. "That's just how it is now."

This is the new normal at NAS Pensacola's main gate. Since March, average wait times during the 6 to 8 a.m. rush have hovered around 45 minutes, according to data provided by Naval Air Station Pensacola Public Affairs. On the worst days, commuters report waits exceeding an hour. The backup regularly extends onto Navy Boulevard, snarling traffic for civilians who aren't even trying to get on base.

The problem, base officials acknowledge, is people. There aren't enough of them checking IDs.

A staffing gap with no quick fix

NAS Pensacola contracts its gate security through a private firm, Paragon Systems, which provides armed guards who verify credentials and inspect vehicles. The base's main gate is authorized for 18 guards per morning shift. Since February, that number has averaged 12.

"We are working closely with our contract partners to address the current staffing shortfall," said Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Foster, public affairs officer for NAS Pensacola, in a statement. "Recruiting and retention challenges in the security sector are affecting installations across the Department of Defense."

Paragon Systems did not respond to requests for comment.

The shortage coincides with new credential verification protocols implemented in January following a security review. Guards must now manually verify each ID holder against an updated database, a process that adds roughly 30 seconds per vehicle. On a morning with 2,000 vehicles passing through, that's an extra 16 hours of processing time spread across available personnel.

"The math just doesn't work," said Marcus Trent, a civilian aircraft mechanic who has worked at the base for 11 years. "You can't add steps to the process and cut the people doing the process and expect it to flow."

Consequences beyond inconvenience

The delays have real costs. Multiple civilian employees interviewed by The Flightline described being marked late or docked pay for tardiness despite leaving home earlier than ever. Contractors working on defense projects say they've lost billable hours sitting in line.

The Naval Hospital reports that patient no-shows for morning appointments have increased 22% since March, according to a hospital spokesperson. Not all of those are attributable to gate delays, the spokesperson said, but "it's a factor we're aware of."

Tom Reyes owns a small electrical contracting firm that does maintenance work on base housing. He said the delays have forced him to restructure his entire workday.

"I used to run a crew through the gate at 7, knock out a job by 10, send them to another site," Reyes said. "Now I tell them, just plan to be on base all day. The gate ate your morning."

Reyes estimated the delays have cost his five-person firm roughly $8,000 in lost productivity since March. He's considering whether base contracts are worth the hassle.

A technological fix, eventually

Navy officials say relief is coming in the form of the Automated Installation Entry system, a credentialing platform that uses encrypted ID cards and vehicle transponders to verify personnel without stopping. The system has been piloted at Naval Station Norfolk and Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam.

NAS Pensacola is scheduled to begin installation in July, with full operation expected by September, according to Lt. Cmdr. Foster.

"AIE will significantly reduce processing time for credentialed personnel while maintaining the highest security standards," Foster said.

The system won't help everyone. Visitors, new employees awaiting permanent credentials and contractors with temporary passes will still require manual processing. Base officials say they're exploring a dedicated visitor lane to prevent those vehicles from slowing credentialed traffic.

But September is four months away. For workers facing the gate every morning, that feels distant.

"They keep saying it's coming," said the nurse in the silver Camry. "I'll believe it when I see it."

Interim measures fall short

In the meantime, the base has implemented what officials call "surge protocols." On Mondays and the first workday after federal holidays—historically the worst days—additional guards are pulled from other posts to supplement the main gate. The base has also extended the hours of the less-trafficked back gate on Blue Angel Parkway, which now opens at 5:30 a.m. instead of 6.

The back gate helps, workers say, but only if you live on the right side of town. For anyone coming from downtown Pensacola or the Perdido Key area, it adds 15 minutes to the drive—often negating any time saved.

"I tried the back gate twice," said Trent, the aircraft mechanic. "By the time I got there, it was backed up too. Everyone had the same idea."

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes areas around the base, said he's heard from constituents about the traffic spillover onto Navy Boulevard. He said he raised the issue with base leadership at a recent community liaison meeting.

"They're aware of it, they're working on it," Bergosh said. "But I told them, my residents who aren't even going on base shouldn't be sitting in that line. There's got to be a better way to stage the traffic."

Base officials said they're coordinating with the Florida Department of Transportation on potential lane reconfigurations for Navy Boulevard, though no timeline has been set.

A problem without villains

No one involved in the situation seems eager to assign blame. Workers are frustrated but sympathetic to the guards, who they describe as professional and working as fast as conditions allow. The guards, for their part, face the stress of an understaffed shift compounded by the impatience of idling commuters.

"I don't blame the guys at the gate," Reyes said. "They're doing their job. The system is broken, not the people."

Lt. Cmdr. Foster emphasized that security cannot be compromised for convenience.

"The safety of everyone who lives and works aboard NAS Pensacola is our highest priority," she said. "We appreciate the patience of our workforce as we implement solutions."

On a recent Wednesday morning, the line at the main gate began forming at 5:45 a.m., 15 minutes before the gate officially opened. By 6:30, it stretched half a mile. The nurse in the Camry had switched to an audiobook—a history of the space race—to pass the time.

"I'm on chapter 12," she said. "I've learned a lot about rockets this month."

The light turned green. The line crept forward. The hospital was still 20 minutes away.
